Space inspires us, and this hackathon is our chance to build something that truly makes a difference.
summary:
Project Harman is an open tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into time-lapse animations of any point in the sky. A user enters a target name (e.g. "R Draconis") or RA/Dec coordinates. The tool queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) through its TAP service, finds every SPHEREx image covering that position, and requests only small server-side cutouts instead of full ~70 MB files. This makes it fast even on slow connections. It then selects the best image for each date and assembles them chronologically into an animated GIF labeled with date and wavelength.

SPHEREx revisits the whole sky roughly every six months. Our tool makes these repeated views visible: nearby high-proper-motion stars and brown dwarfs (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855) shift position, and variable stars (RW Aurigae, R Draconis) change brightness. Hunting for faint moving objects, including a hypothetical Planet X, starts with exactly this kind of multi-epoch comparison. Harman makes it accessible to students and citizen scientists with no astronomy software, no API keys and no downloads of huge files
details:
What it does
Project Harman creates time-lapse animations of any point in the sky from NASA's SPHEREx survey. The user enters a target name (e.g. "R Draconis", resolved via astronomical name catalogs) or RA/Dec coordinates, a field of view, a wavelength and the number of frames. The output is an animated GIF in which each frame shows the same patch of sky on a different date, labeled with the observation date and wavelength.

How it works

  1. Search: The tool sends an ADQL query to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) TAP service and lists all SPHEREx images (spherex.obscore) near the target in the chosen wavelength range.
  2. Filter: Using each image's footprint polygon (s_region), it keeps only images that truly contain the target. It groups them by date and ranks candidates by distance from the image center, where image quality is best.
  3. Download smartly: Instead of full ~70 MB files, it requests small server-side cutouts from IRSA (typically a few hundred KB). That is more than 100 times less data. If the server rejects a cutout size, it retries with a smaller one.
  4. Process: Each cutout is centered on the target with Astropy (WCS + Cutout2D). Frames with too much missing data are rejected. Brightness is scaled with an asinh stretch so faint sources stay visible.
  5. Animate: Frames are sorted chronologically, evenly sampled across the full time range, labeled,and saved as a looping GIF.

Benefits and impact
SPHEREx maps the entire sky about every six months. Comparing these epochs reveals nearby stars and brown dwarfs moving across the sky, as well as variable stars changing brightness. This multi-epoch comparison is the same basic method used to search for faint, slow-moving objects such as a hypothetical Planet X. Harman makes it possible for students, teachers and citizen scientists to see this themselves, with no astronomy software, no API keys and no gigabyte downloads.

Tools and technologies
Python, Astropy (coordinates, FITS, WCS, Cutout2D), NumPy, Requests (with automatic retries), Pillow (GIF generation), the IRSA TAP service with ADQL, IVOA DataLink, IRSA's cutout service, Git/GitHub and VS Code.

What makes it creative
SPHEREx was designed as a spectral survey. We use its repeated coverage in a different way: as a "time machine" for the infrared sky. The server-side cutout approach lets the tool run even on slow mobile connections.

Factors we considered

  • Bandwidth: cutouts instead of full images.
  • Reliability: automatic retries, a fallback candidate image for each date, and graceful handling of server errors.
  • Respect for NASA's servers: limited parallel downloads and short pauses between requests.
  • Scientific honesty: we only use images whose footprint actually contains the target, and every frame shows its true observation date.

Next steps
Aligning all frames to a common north-up grid, difference images that highlight motion, brightness-over-time light curves, and a web interface.
